This paper investigates the modulus of a polynomial $P(z)$ in the immediate vicinity of a point $z_0$ where $P(z_0)=0$. We demonstrate that the zero's behavior is partitioned into $\pi/k$ sectors, where $k$ represents the multiplicity of the zero at $z_0$. Within each sector, the magnitude follows a distinct power law, $|P(z)| \sim |z-z_0|^{\alpha}$, with the exponent $\alpha$ determined by the specific coefficients of the polynomial. We derive these exponents for polynomials of degree up to four and provide numerical illustrations for higher degrees. Furthermore, we examine the scenario involving multiple zeros of varying multiplicities clustered in close proximity.

This study examines the stability of one-dimensional bright solitons within a Bose-Einstein condensate featuring both attractive dipole-dipole interactions and self-focusing nonlinearities. We analyze both contact and dipolar regimes, deriving a stability criterion for bright solitons in terms of the relative strengths of attractive dipole-dipole interactions and self-focusing nonlinearities. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of these solitons under a perturbation, demonstrating that they remain stable within a specific parameter range.

This paper introduces a novel optimization framework for deriving the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality, featuring a generalized function that extends the standard geometric-arithmetic mean. The study establishes the convexity of this extended function, applies the framework to prove the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality, and demonstrates its equivalence to the classic result.

We introduce a manifold-based generalization of the Birman exact sequence, which extends the classical result known for surfaces. This new sequence connects the mapping class group $\mathcal{M}_{g,b}$ of the Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}_{g,b}$ (associated with a $g$-punctured genus-$g$ surface and $b$ boundary components) with the corresponding topological Teichmüller space $\mathcal{T}^{top}_{g,b}$. Specifically, the sequence is expressed as:
$$1 \rightarrow \mathcal{T}^{top}_{g,b} \rightarrow \mathcal{M}_{g,b} \rightarrow \mathcal{T}_{g,b} \rightarrow 1$$
Here, $\mathcal{T}^{top}_{g,b}$ denotes the fundamental groupoid of $\mathcal{T}_{g,b}$, which we define as the groupoid of isotopy classes of diffeomorphisms of $\mathcal{T}_{g,b}$ that fix the boundary components pointwise. This sequence is derived from the exact sequence of the fundamental groupoid of the punctured torus, extended to the general case of $\mathcal{T}_{g,b}$.

RGB-D sequences offer a cost-effective and straightforward method for capturing human motion and appearance, making them ideal for generating personalized virtual avatars. This paper introduces a new framework for creating personalized 3D human avatars from RGB-D data. Our approach employs a dual-stream architecture: a 3D geometry network that reconstructs body shape and pose, and a 2D appearance network that synthesizes skin and clothing textures. To ensure high-quality avatar generation, we have developed a specialized loss function that optimizes both the 3D structure and 2D appearance. Experiments demonstrate that our method produces superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Reconstructing 3D facial models from images is a critical task in computer vision, with applications ranging from virtual reality to medical imaging. However, this process is often hindered by occlusions, such as masks or hands, which can severely compromise the accuracy of the resulting 3D models. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning the implicit representation of 3D face geometry and texture from a single image, specifically designed to handle these challenging occlusions. By leveraging a pre-trained 3D face model, we utilize a differentiable renderer to generate synthetic training data, enabling the training of a neural network that maps a single image to an interpretable 3D face model. This approach allows for the seamless reconstruction of faces even when partially obscured. Extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in reconstructing faces from occluded images.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm where agents learn to maximize cumulative rewards through interactions with their environment. A central challenge in RL is balancing exploration and exploitation, a dilemma that has been addressed using various methods. This paper introduces a novel approach to this issue by leveraging the concept of mutual information. We demonstrate that mutual information can quantify the degree of exploration and propose a new exploration bonus grounded in this metric. The effectiveness of our proposed method is validated through experiments on three standard RL benchmarks.

This study introduces a novel framework for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that integrates the strengths of both centralized training and decentralized execution. By utilizing a centralized architecture during the policy optimization phase, the proposed method ensures effective action selection, while employing a decentralized execution enables autonomous operation. The core mechanism relies on a local action space decomposition strategy, where each agent optimizes its policy conditioned on the actions of others within the set. This localized approach facilitates the emergence of globally optimal policies, as it allows individual agents to identify optimal moves for their specific action subsets. The framework is validated through experiments in a multi-agent card game, demonstrating its efficacy in achieving superior performance.

This study examines the rapidity gap phenomenon in proton-proton collisions, specifically focusing on the region separating two leading jets. We present a theoretical framework for this effect, which is derived from a specific subset of next-to-leading order (NLO) QCD corrections. Our analysis incorporates both the $2 \to 2$ and $2 \to 3$ scattering processes. We demonstrate that this approach is fully consistent with the NLO QCD framework, as it correctly reproduces the total cross-section. Furthermore, we provide predictions for the cross-section distribution as a function of the rapidity gap.

Silicene, a two-dimensional silicon analogue, has garnered significant attention due to its exceptional thermoelectric (TE) capabilities. This study investigates the TE characteristics of penta-silicene, a newly discovered two-dimensional silicon allotrope. Our findings indicate that this material exhibits a high Seebeck coefficient of 200 $\mu$V/K at room temperature, driven by its unique electronic band structure. Furthermore, the combination of high electrical conductivity and low lattice thermal conductivity results in a superior dimensionless figure of merit (ZT) of 1.1 at room temperature. Consequently, penta-silicene emerges as a promising candidate for high-efficiency TE applications.

This study investigates the charmonium and bottomonium dissociation mechanisms within a hot magnetized environment by employing the AdS/CFT correspondence. We specifically examine the spectral properties of heavy quarkonia in this hot magnetized plasma by analyzing the dynamics of a heavy quark-antiquark pair linked by a linearly confining string within a five-dimensional AdS black hole spacetime featuring a uniform external magnetic field. Our findings indicate that the binding energies of charmonium and bottomonium states are influenced by the combined effects of the temperature and the magnetic field intensity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dissociation of quarkonia in this medium is governed by the interplay between the temperature and the magnetic field.

This study examines the potential for detecting dark matter (DM) interactions with Standard Model particles by analyzing the light curves of various astronomical events. We specifically investigate the impact of DM-DM annihilation products on the light curves of Type Ia supernovae, solar flares, and gamma-ray bursts. By utilizing the latest observational data, we establish stringent new constraints on the DM annihilation cross-section across a broad spectrum of DM masses. Our findings indicate that the cross-sections derived from solar flares and gamma-ray bursts are comparable to those from supernovae, with supernovae offering the distinct advantage of covering a significantly wider mass range. Consequently, we conclude that the combined analysis of these three sources yields the most robust and comprehensive constraints on the DM annihilation cross-section.

Green Security Games (GSGs) offer a framework for safeguarding valuable assets, such as natural resources, from dynamic threats. This approach involves an agent managing a team of mobile guards to protect the asset against an adversary capable of causing irreversible damage. This paper introduces a novel GSG variant where the agent employs a mixed strategy to decide between deploying guards or allowing the adversary to attack. We demonstrate that this strategy maximizes the agent's utility by balancing the costs of guard deployment against the high utility derived from successfully protecting the asset. Furthermore, we prove that a Nash equilibrium exists for this game structure.

This paper introduces a new approach for enabling robots to navigate rough landscapes by leveraging the attention mechanism. The method constructs an attention map by synthesizing data from a terrain roughness model, a depth sensor, and an elevation model. Subsequently, this attention map is converted into an attention mask that directs the robot's path planning. The system's efficacy is validated through a series of simulations and a physical field test conducted on a six-wheeled robot traversing a mountainous landscape.

The study of magnetic systems is fundamentally driven by the competition between disorder, frustration, and anisotropy. In this work, we investigate the interplay between uniaxial anisotropy and frustration within the context of the spin-1/2 triangular antiferromagnetic lattice. By employing a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and exact diagonalization, we demonstrate that uniaxial anisotropy can simultaneously reduce both disorder and frustration. This finding challenges the conventional perspective that anisotropy primarily mitigates frustration, a view that has historically been the dominant focus in the field.

This study examines the inverse problem of identifying a planar conductivity inclusion within a background medium using a single measurement of a generalized polarization tensor (GPT). We demonstrate that for simply connected domains, this single GPT measurement suffices to determine the inclusion's shape and conductivity uniquely. Furthermore, we prove that the gradient of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map evaluated at a specific point encapsulates all necessary information regarding the inclusion's geometry and material properties.

The stability of magnetic fields within stars is a critical issue in stellar astrophysics, as these fields can trigger instabilities that alter stellar evolution. This study examines the stability of axisymmetric magnetic fields in a rotating, incompressible, rotating star. We demonstrate that a broad spectrum of axisymmetric magnetic field configurations are susceptible to instability. Specifically, we establish that if the magnetic field is poloidal, the toroidal component of the magnetic field must be unstable. Conversely, if the toroidal component is absent, the poloidal field must be unstable. These findings are derived from the energy principle, which is a method for analyzing the stability of magnetic fields in a rotating, incompressible, rotating star. We also show that the energy principle can be used to determine the stability of magnetic fields in a rotating, incompressible, rotating star.

Synchronization in networks is a fundamental phenomenon with broad applications, yet it remains a challenging problem when extending beyond standard graph structures. This study investigates the synchronization of Kuramoto oscillators on simplicial complexes, a generalization of graphs that incorporates higher-order interactions. We demonstrate that the synchronization capacity of such complexes is governed by their spectral dimension, a metric derived from the eigenvalue distribution of the Laplacian operator. Specifically, we prove that complete synchronization is guaranteed if the spectral dimension exceeds 4. Conversely, for spectral dimensions lower than 4, the system exhibits mixed states characterized by the coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized components. These findings are supported by numerical simulations.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and linear systems solvers are fundamental components in numerous scientific and engineering domains, including computational fluid dynamics, structural analysis, and machine learning. These tools are essential for accelerating research and development. However, the performance of SpMV and iterative solvers is often constrained by memory bandwidth limitations. This paper introduces a novel SpMV architecture designed to enhance performance by leveraging a specialized sparse matrix format. The proposed design employs a custom, high-performance memory format that organizes data into 128-bit blocks, each containing 16 32-bit floating-point numbers. This approach significantly reduces memory access overhead by aligning data storage with the vector registers of modern GPUs. Additionally, the work presents a GPU-optimized implementation of the Conjugate Gradient (CG) solver, which integrates the new matrix format to boost SpMV efficiency. Experimental results indicate that this GPU-based solver achieves a speedup of 1.5x to 2.5x over existing GPU implementations.

Let $F$ denote a collection of meromorphic functions defined on a domain $D$, and let $H$ be a non-empty set of meromorphic values. Suppose there exists a normal family $G$ on $D$ containing only non-constant limit functions that shares the set $H$ with $F$ through partial sharing. Specifically, for each $g \in G$, there is a corresponding $f \in F$ such that $g \equiv^* f$ relative to $H$. Under these conditions, we demonstrate that $F$ possesses a normal character.

Human teams often collaborate to achieve a common goal, a process that can be modeled as "intention sharing." This process involves two distinct types: "individual intentions," where each member aims to complete their specific task, and a "common intention," which requires the entire team to reach a collective objective. This research introduces a framework for intention sharing within human-robot teams, specifically designed to foster collaboration. The approach utilizes a multi-agent decision-making model to derive a shared plan, which is then executed through the intention-based shared planning (ISSP) architecture. To evaluate this framework, we conducted a simulation involving a human-robot team tasked with delivering a package to a target location. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework successfully generates a shared plan and effectively executes it, thereby supporting human-robot teamwork.

This work examines the geometry of decomposable Monge-Ampère systems within complex projective hypersurfaces of $\mathbb{P}^n$ and establishes a link between their Lagrangian pairs and Hodge theory. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Hodge locus of any Lagrangian pair embedded in $\mathbb{P}^n$ constitutes the complete Hodge locus associated with the associated bi-decomposable Monge-Ampère system. Furthermore, we prove that the compactification of the local moduli space for such systems on $\mathbb{P}^n$ is precisely the Jacobian compactified Jacobian of a specific smooth curve in $\mathbb{P}^n$.

Electrolysis of water is a promising method for generating hydrogen and oxygen, yet it remains hindered by sluggish bubble growth and shrinkage dynamics. This study investigates the influence of bubble spacing on growth rates through a numerical model that accounts for the two-phase flow of gas bubbles and liquid electrolyte. The model incorporates bubble nucleation, growth, and detachment, alongside the effects of bubble coalescence and interfacial electrochemical reactions. Simulations were conducted in a two-dimensional channel with a 100 μm width, featuring a 100 μm wide electrode. The results indicate that coalescence is a critical factor governing bubble growth rates. Specifically, when bubble spacing is less than 100 μm, the growth rate is primarily dictated by coalescence, whereas larger spacing results in growth rates controlled by the electrochemical reaction.

This study examines the production of a pair of long-lived particles (LLPs) in high-energy proton-proton collisions, where each LLP decays into a pair of Standard Model charged leptons. The analysis focuses on events containing two oppositely charged lepton pairs, each accompanied by missing transverse momentum, with the LLPs traveling proper decay lengths ranging from 100 micrometers to 10 meters. The investigation utilizes data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. No significant excess beyond the Standard Model background is observed, allowing for the establishment of upper limits on the cross-section times branching fraction. These findings are used to constrain the parameter space of a simplified model describing LLP production via Drell-Yan processes and their subsequent decays into leptons.

We examine the low-energy effective theory of a second-order Dirac semimetal characterized by anisotropy and finite dispersion. At low energies, the system's behavior is governed by a nonlinear renormalization group equation for the coupling constant and anisotropy parameters. We demonstrate that the renormalization group flow drives the coupling constant toward zero, indicating that the second-order Dirac semimetal is an asymptotically free state. Furthermore, we identify a specific critical energy scale where the anisotropy parameters undergo a qualitative shift.

This paper introduces a new methodology for designing concurrent data structure operations, which derives from a high-level, commonsense description of the intended behavior. The approach employs a novel formalism of concurrent commonsense reasoning to represent these descriptions. It then utilizes a sound and relatively complete compilation algorithm to convert this reasoning into concurrent operations that guarantee correctness. Furthermore, the methodology incorporates an efficient optimization strategy that leverages the semantics of the commonsense description to generate operations which are both more concise and more performant than traditional alternatives.

Superconducting containers enable the magnetic levitation of neodymium ferromagnets via the Meissner effect. This phenomenon permits the creation of a compact, mobile, and highly stable magnetic field source, which can be integrated into electronic circuits. We present a method for fabricating these superconducting vessels using a straightforward photolithographic process. The resulting traps successfully levitated a 1.5 cm³ neodymium magnet with a mass of 20 g, maintaining stability for durations exceeding 100 seconds. Additionally, we demonstrate the circuit's utility by connecting the superconducting trap to a SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) to detect the magnetic field generated by the levitated magnet.

We report the detection of ethynyl benzene (C$_6$H$_5$C$_2$H) in the hot molecular core of the massive protostar W3(OH) using the IRAM 30m telescope. The source is identified through a distinctive rotational ladder of 11 transitions spanning 10.5 to 11.6 GHz, with the J$_{11,10}$ line peaking at 11.5 GHz and reaching an intensity of 0.12 mK. The derived column density is $N_{\rm col} = (1.6 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$, and the rotational temperature is estimated at 100 K. The observed column density aligns with the expected abundance for a hot core species, and the rotational temperature is consistent with the thermal conditions of the surrounding hot molecular core.

We investigate the potential for asymmetric dark matter (ADM) to generate detectable gravitational waves (GWs) by examining the formation of compact objects within the dark sector. Specifically, we analyze a model where dark matter consists of a scalar particle and a dark baryon, both interacting via a dark force. While the scalar dark matter component can collapse to form a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC), the dark baryons are hypothesized to form compact stars. We examine the formation of these objects during the asymmetric dark matter epoch and calculate the resulting GW emission. Our analysis indicates that the GW signals from the collapse of dark BECs and the formation of compact stars could potentially be detected by future GW observatories.

This study reports the first measurement of the $t\bar{t}Z$ process cross section using data from proton-proton collisions at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on the four-lepton final state, where the $t\bar{t}Z$ signal is extracted from the background of the standard $t\bar{t}$ process by applying a selection requiring a $Z$ boson decaying into electrons or muons. The resulting measured cross section is $\sigma_{t\bar{t}Z} = 1.00^{+0.38}_{-0.34}$ pb. This value aligns with Standard Model predictions, with the uncertainty representing a combination of statistical and systematic components.

We categorize the orbits of real two-tuples under the action of the group $\mathbb{R}^*\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})^4$. This classification yields three distinct types of orbits, which are then utilized to define a canonical basis for the space of real two-tuples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the canonical basis corresponding to the most general case possesses exactly three distinct elements.

Predictive State Representations (PSRs) offer a robust framework for modeling partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) by focusing on predictions regarding future observations. Unlike traditional methods, PSRs do not require modeling hidden states, thereby eliminating the need for explicit state estimation. However, PSRs are inherently limited to passive observation and lack the capacity to handle control and planning tasks. To address this, we introduce a novel class of generative models called Generative Predictive State Representations (GPSRs). These models extend the capabilities of PSRs to handle sequential decision-making under partial observability. We demonstrate that GPSRs can be derived from standard POMDPs and are capable of accurately predicting observations following any sequence of actions. Furthermore, we establish a formal link between GPSRs and POMDPs, proving that GPSRs can be trained directly from environmental interaction data without access to the underlying POMDP structure.

Gentrification, a widespread phenomenon in cities, often triggers significant social challenges such as displacement, rising crime, and deteriorating living standards. To address these issues, researchers have developed various methods to detect and monitor gentrification, yet most existing approaches rely on large-scale, high-resolution data that are costly to acquire. This paper introduces a novel methodology for identifying gentrification using low-resolution satellite imagery, specifically targeting areas with limited data availability. Our approach utilizes a deep learning framework to estimate neighborhood characteristics—such as housing prices, crime rates, and income levels—from satellite data, followed by the application of a clustering algorithm to identify gentrified zones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through case studies in New York City and Chicago, utilizing satellite data from the Landsat 8 satellite.

We present a theoretical framework for a chiral magnet exhibiting a topological skyrmion lattice that undergoes a phase transition into a ferromagnetic state with a non-collinear spin texture. This transition is driven by the interplay between the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction and the magnetocrystalline anisotropy. We demonstrate that the ferromagnetic phase supports a ground-state configuration of finite energy, characterized by a non-collinear spin arrangement. Furthermore, we calculate the energy of this texture and analyze its stability.

This paper studies composition operators within harmonic-$Q_{k,q}$ spaces (a subset of harmonic-Bloch type spaces) defined on the unit disk. We determine necessary and sufficient conditions for these operators to be bounded and to belong to the classes of compact and Dunford–Pettit operators.

The transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is a key strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and mitigating climate change. Nevertheless, the environmental sustainability of EVs relies heavily on the carbon intensity of the electricity grid, which varies significantly by region. To address this, range-extended electric vehicles (REV) offer a flexible alternative by enabling battery recharging via alternative sources, such as hydrogen fuel cells. This study evaluates the environmental impact of REV compared to conventional internal combustion engines (ICE) and standard EVs, specifically examining the potential for hydrogen production through electrolysis powered by renewable energy. The research employs a life cycle assessment (LCA) utilizing the openLCA framework to analyze these vehicle types. Results indicate that the REV achieves the lowest environmental footprint, followed by the standard EV, with the traditional ICE vehicle exhibiting the highest impact.

We present a study of heavy-quark mesons within the framework of the Schwinger-Dyson equations, utilizing a model for the gluon propagator that incorporates infrared enhancement. This approach is contrasted with a scenario where the propagator is treated as a constant. We demonstrate that the infrared enhancement is essential for reproducing the experimentally observed mass spectra of heavy-quark mesons. Furthermore, we argue that the dressing functions must exhibit flavor dependence to accurately describe the full spectrum of heavy-quark mesons.

This study introduces a novel numerical approach for subsurface flow applications that overcomes the challenges posed by highly heterogeneous media. The method employs a time-stepping strategy to discretize history effects, while spatial discretization is handled by the discontinuous Galerkin finite element method (DG-FEM). This combination allows for the efficient simulation of subsurface processes in complex environments.

This paper introduces a deep learning approach for predicting the motion of surrounding vehicles in autonomous driving scenarios. By utilizing a deep neural network, the proposed method forecasts the future trajectories of other road users based on their recent historical paths. The system's efficacy is evaluated by comparing its predictions against ground truth data collected from a real-world driving simulator.

This study examines the low-temperature characteristics of GaN MESFETs, specifically focusing on the impact of trap centers on the drain current. The analysis utilizes a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model that incorporates a trap-assisted tunneling current model. The results indicate that trap centers significantly influence device performance at low temperatures, causing a notable reduction in the threshold voltage and transconductance, alongside a marked increase in drain current. The research further explores the relationship between trap density and the device's transconductance and threshold voltage, providing insights into the underlying physical mechanisms. The findings suggest that optimizing trap density could lead to enhanced device performance, particularly in applications requiring operation at cryogenic temperatures. The study concludes by highlighting the potential for future work to explore the role of trap centers in the development of high-performance GaN MESFETs for space and cryogenic applications. The work provides valuable information for researchers and engineers seeking to understand and mitigate the adverse effects of trap centers on GaN MESFET performance at low temperatures. The study also offers a comprehensive understanding of the physical processes governing GaN MESFET behavior under cryogenic conditions, which is crucial for the design and optimization of these devices for specialized applications. The findings contribute to the broader understanding of GaN MESFET physics and their potential for advanced technological applications. The study's conclusions are supported by a detailed analysis of the device's electrical characteristics, offering a robust foundation for future research and development in the field of GaN MESFET technology.

Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are essential for numerous applications, yet their performance degrades in urban settings due to multipath effects, signal attenuation, and interference. These challenges lead to unreliable measurements, resulting in degraded positioning accuracy and navigation errors. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance GNSS positioning by integrating a deep learning-based denoising module with a particle filter for position estimation. The proposed architecture employs a deep neural network to identify and remove multipath errors from pseudorange and carrier phase data, followed by the particle filter to generate the final position estimate. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly improves positioning accuracy compared to standard techniques.

This study introduces a new framework for analyzing high-dimensional tensor-variate data, which is characterized by multiple modes. We present the Sylvester generative model, which is grounded in the concept of a multilinear map. This model is capable of capturing the interdependencies among the various modes within a tensor. Furthermore, it offers a flexible approach for modeling complex, non-Gaussian distributions. We develop an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm designed to estimate the parameters of this model. Additionally, we demonstrate the model's theoretical consistency and its computational efficiency through both extensive simulations and a real-world application.

This study introduces a vision system designed for tracking fast-moving objects using event cameras. The approach integrates event-based tracking with deep learning techniques to generate a point cloud of the target, which is subsequently projected onto a 2D image plane. The methodology employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the event stream, followed by a deep learning model that processes these features to predict the object's 2D position and orientation. The system's efficacy is validated through experiments tracking a tennis ball in flight.

This paper introduces a novel framework for multi-level cache-enabled networks, where caches are strategically deployed at various nodes to enhance efficiency. The study investigates a multi-level caching architecture comprising a base station, multiple access points (APs), and user equipment (UEs), each equipped with varying cache capacities. The authors develop a novel multi-level caching allocation strategy designed to maximize network-wide hit rates. The problem is initially addressed in a static setting, where the cache sizes of the base station, APs, and UEs are fixed, and the optimal hit rate is derived. Subsequently, the research extends to a dynamic setting, where these cache sizes can be adjusted. The authors propose a two-stage algorithm to optimize the hit rate in this dynamic environment. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this proposed method achieves a significantly higher hit rate compared to existing approaches.

We demonstrate a proof for the PPT square conjecture, showing that any positive partial transpose (PPT) squared operator in a finite-dimensional $4 \times 4$ matrix space is inherently positive definite. This finding confirms a recent conjecture proposed by Wang and Wang in *Communications in Number Theory and Physics* (2020, Vol. 14, pp. 351–358).

A normal edge-transitive Cayley graph $\Gamma$ is defined such that its automorphism group $G$ is both edge-transitive and contains an edge-transitive subgroup of the Cayley group that normalizes the underlying Cayley group. This paper establishes a condition for the existence of such graphs: there exists a normal edge-transitive Cayley graph with group $G$ if and only if $G$ possesses a generating set $\{x, y\}$ where $y$ is an involution and $x$ has an order that is a prime number.

This paper addresses the problem of selecting a set of anchors for localization tasks, such as navigation and robot control, by minimizing the worst-case Dilution of Precision (DOP). The proposed method introduces a novel, computationally efficient algorithm that utilizes a geometric approach to anchor selection. This approach transforms the anchor selection challenge into a geometric optimization problem, specifically a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), which can be solved efficiently using branch-and-bound techniques. Additionally, we introduce a streamlined method to calculate the DOP for any given anchor configuration. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through extensive simulations, which show that the proposed worst-case DOP minimization yields superior results compared to existing methods.

This study introduces a novel approach to calculating the Debye temperature ($\Theta_D$) for condensed matter systems, utilizing the shear modulus ($G$) alongside the linear sound velocity ($v_l$) and transverse sound velocity ($v_t$). The proposed method demonstrates strong agreement with existing experimental data across various materials. Furthermore, it offers a means to determine $\Theta_D$ for amorphous substances, which are typically difficult to characterize experimentally. The reliability of this method is validated by its consistency with both empirical observations and theoretical predictions.

Deep learning-based motion deblurring techniques typically rely on synthetic datasets that pair clear images with simulated blurry versions. However, these datasets often fail to accurately replicate the blur characteristics found in real-world images, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce a new deep learning framework for motion deblurring that utilizes synthetic blur data and a dedicated blur enhancement module. This module is designed to automatically refine the synthetic blurry images, ensuring they align more closely with actual physical blur patterns present in real scenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving superior results in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) occur when supermassive black holes (SMBHs) in galaxies disrupt stars, a process that may illuminate the nature of black holes in the early universe. While the rate of such events is expected to decline as galaxies evolve, the specific decline in the rate of tidal disruption events (TDEs) as a function of redshift remains uncertain. This study utilizes the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) to identify 11 candidate TDEs at redshifts greater than 0.5, including one at $z=0.91$. By analyzing the redshift distribution of these candidates alongside the known SMBH mass function, we find that the TDE rate drops by a factor of 10 between $z=0.5$ and $z=0.1$. This observed decline aligns with the hypothesis that the rate of tidal disruption events tracks the star formation rate of their host galaxies.

The reionization epoch is marked by a complex, heterogeneous process of Ly$\alpha$ photon escape from galaxies, which is heavily influenced by their immediate surroundings. This study examines the transmission of Ly$\alpha$ light from 10,000 galaxies within the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulation, specifically targeting those with redshifts between 6.5 and 7.5 and stellar masses exceeding $10^{9.5} M_{\odot}$. We analyze the transmission profiles across a $100 h^{-1}$ Mpc radius around each target, categorizing the local environments based on the presence of ionized bubbles and the fraction of neutral hydrogen. Our findings reveal that while neutral hydrogen fraction is the primary determinant of transmission, the existence of ionized bubbles significantly enhances it. Specifically, we observe that Ly$\alpha$ photons experience a 1.5-fold increase in transmission when emitted from galaxies situated within ionized bubbles compared to those in identical conditions within non-bubbly regions.

The study of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) has been significantly advanced by the Gaia mission, which has provided a comprehensive photometric survey of the sky. This work introduces a novel method for determining the color of TNOs by utilizing the Gaia $G_{BP}$ and $G_{RP}$ filters alongside the $Z$-band from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). We applied this technique to 10 cold classical TNOs, including 2018 SC 12, 2021 PZ10, 2022 KP7, 2022 QF10, 2022 QF11, 2022 QF12, 2022 QF13, 2022 QF14, 2022 QF15, 2022 QF16, 2022 QF17, 2022 QF18, 2022 QF19, 2022 QF20, 2022 QF21, 2022 QF22, 2022 QF23, 2022 QF24, 2022 QF25, 2022 QF26,

This study examines the critical shear stress (CRSS) for the $\alpha \to \omega$ phase transformation in Ti-6Al alloys across a temperature range from 298 to 473 K. By analyzing the temperature dependence of CRSS, we have identified the specific thermodynamic and kinetic parameters necessary to model this transformation.

Software Product Lines (SPLs) are characterized by a shared core augmented with diverse variations. Feature Models serve as the primary tool for representing these variations, depicting the relationships among various features. While model checking is a well-established technique for analyzing Feature Models, it is often limited to small-scale models due to the state explosion problem. This paper introduces a model checking approach for Feature Models that leverages the SMT solver Z3. The proposed method translates the verification query into an Satisfiability (SAT) problem, which is then resolved using a SAT solver. The authors evaluate this technique by applying it to verify two specific properties: feature dependency and feature coherence.

We introduce a novel method for determining completeness in high contrast imaging, designed to evaluate the ability of the SPHERE instrument to detect faint companions. This approach involves injecting simulated point sources into real images and analyzing their recovery rates. By employing a parallel, automated pipeline, we generate numerous test cases to assess completeness across various separation and magnitude combinations. Our findings indicate that the SPHERE/ZIMPRES completeness model, which relies on a single reference image, is insufficient for accurately determining completeness. Instead, we propose a new model that incorporates the specific instrumental point spread function (PSF) of each observation. This refined model demonstrates superior accuracy, with a mean absolute error of 0.13 magnitudes and a mean absolute flux error of 0.11.

We investigate the dynamics of a Schwarzschild black hole evaporating via Hawking radiation within a fixed charge background. This process is analyzed through symmetry-resolved entropies, which quantify the information held by an observer about the radiation emitted in specific charge sectors. Our analysis demonstrates that the entanglement entropy for each charge sector exhibits a distinct three-phase structure. We further examine the implications of these findings for black hole evaporation and discuss their relevance to various information paradox scenarios.

The Weyl semimetal candidate ZrSiAs was recently identified as hosting a Fermi arc. This study examines the topological characteristics of the Fermi surface in ZrSiAs using a tight-binding model, revealing that the arc originates from the nontrivial nature of the band structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the arc is robust against perturbations, including those from spin-orbit coupling, and that the arc's presence is closely linked to the specific arrangement of the Weyl nodes.

Video prediction remains a difficult challenge, primarily because of the intricate relationships between pixels across both space and time. While recent advancements have shown that transformer-based models can achieve high-quality video predictions, they typically depend on large-scale training datasets. In this paper, we introduce a novel training approach that enables the effective transfer of knowledge from a pre-trained model to a specific target domain. Our method leverages a multi-scale feature fusion strategy to capture both local and global information, facilitating the learning of spatiotemporal dependencies. Furthermore, we employ a multi-task learning framework to enhance the model's predictive performance. Extensive experiments conducted on the DAVIS, UCF101, and UCF-ShortNet datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art video prediction methods.

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are linked to both aging and various diseases. Although the specific mitochondrial mutations that characterize healthy aging remain unclear, this study investigates the role of mitochondrial mutations in the aging process by analyzing a cohort of 1,000 individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project. This paper introduces a novel mel-spectrogram-based end-to-end speech synthesis framework. It employs a non-autoregressive model to generate mel-spectograms from text and acoustic features, which are subsequently converted into speech waveforms using a vocoder. To address the challenges inherent in non-autoregressive speech synthesis, we propose a new multi-head attention mechanism that captures long-term dependencies within mel frames. Additionally, we introduce a new loss function designed to enhance the quality of generated mel-spectograms. Experimental results indicate that this approach produces speech with superior perceptual quality compared to prior work.

Ge-Sb-Te (GST) alloys are widely utilized in phase-change memory applications due to their ability to switch between amorphous and crystalline states, which exhibit distinct electrical and optical characteristics. This study employs density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the electronic structure of amorphous and crystalline phases of the Ge2Sb2Te5 alloy. The analysis reveals that the material's electronic structure is primarily dictated by Ge and Sb atoms, with the Ge-5s and Sb-5s orbitals forming the valence band maximum and the Ge-6p orbitals forming the conduction band minimum. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the material's electronic structure is highly sensitive to the local atomic environment, a factor that significantly influences the material's optical properties.

We introduce a framework for the 3+1 dimensional fractional topological insulator (FTI) that arises from the interplay between fractionalization and the quantum anomaly of a discrete symmetry. This approach is realized through a compact bosonic theory featuring a $U(1)^3$ global symmetry, which is spontaneously broken into a residual $U(1)^2$ subgroup. The resulting vacuum supports a mixed anomaly between the emergent $U(1)^2$ symmetry and spatial reflection symmetry $S_x$. This anomaly drives the fractionalization mechanism, giving rise to a 3D topological insulator phase. The FTI exhibits a gapped, non-chiral topological surface state, which is protected by the mixed anomaly. We demonstrate that this phase can be described by a bosonic Chern-Simons theory with a mixed term, and we show that the anomaly can be realized using a lattice model of interacting bosons.

We present a 3D radiation-hydrodynamics simulation of a protoplanetary disc featuring a central cavity, which is crucial for understanding planet formation. This study employs a novel methodology that integrates a 3D radiation-hydrodynamics framework with a 3D radiative transfer solver, enabling the self-consistent modeling of gas dynamics and thermal evolution. The disc is initialized with a central hole and a density gradient that increases outward, a configuration typical of discs observed in ALMA studies. Our results indicate that the gas dynamics are primarily governed by viscous evolution, with gas accretion onto the central star and subsequent disc spreading. The gas temperature is determined by the balance between viscous heating and radiative cooling. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed for high-dimensional observations, characterized by inherent sparsity. The approach employs data augmentation to generate a latent representation that captures the underlying low-dimensional structure, thereby enabling the effective application of existing reinforcement learning algorithms. We demonstrate that our method offers significant advantages over direct RL application on raw data, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical results across multiple tasks.

Arabic serves as a major global language with approximately 300 million speakers, yet it remains underrepresented in the field of natural language processing. This study introduces a novel dataset named "Arabic Sentiment Corpus" (ASC), which consists of 1.2 million manually annotated Arabic sentences labeled with positive, negative, or neutral sentiments. The annotation process involved a rigorous three-stage review to ensure high quality. Furthermore, the corpus underwent evaluation using a state-of-the-art deep learning model, demonstrating that the dataset is suitable for Sentiment Analysis (SA) tasks.

The Guillotine Strip Packing problem involves arranging a set of rectangles with integer dimensions into a strip of fixed width to minimize the total height. This problem is defined by a constraint requiring that any rectangular placement can be separated from the rest of the layout via a single straight cut. While numerous approximation algorithms exist for the Strip Packing problem, the specific performance of the Guillotine variant remains less explored. This paper introduces a novel approximation algorithm for the Guillotine Strip Packing problem, achieving an approximation ratio of $1.25 + \varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

We introduce a novel technique for estimating galaxy cluster masses by analyzing Compton-y parameter maps. This approach utilizes a machine learning model trained on simulations that replicate the cosmological conditions of the target survey. The model is designed to map Compton-y maps to cluster masses, achieving a precision of approximately 10% for clusters with masses exceeding $10^{14} M_{\odot}$. This level of accuracy surpasses the current best methods, which rely on scaling relations derived from X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) data. Furthermore, our proposed method is independent of assumptions regarding the cluster formation process.

Topic modeling serves as a potent instrument for uncovering latent structures within extensive datasets. However, applying this technique to languages lacking distinct word boundaries, such as classical Chinese, remains challenging. This study introduces tokenization strategies—specifically Pearson's chi-squared test and t-statistics—to segment classical Chinese characters into meaningful units. We subsequently employed the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model to evaluate the efficacy of these methods. The findings indicate that both the Pearson's chi-squared test and t-statistics are viable approaches for segmenting classical Chinese characters.

This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to identify pulsar candidates within the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array (PPoTA) dataset. The PPoTA data comprises 1,000 hours of observations from the Parkes radio telescope, encompassing 1,000 pulsars and 1,000,000 noise-only intervals. The PPoTA dataset is characterized by a class imbalance problem, as the number of pulsar signals is significantly lower than the number of noise-only intervals. The PPoTA framework employs a multi-stage approach to identify pulsar signals, using a combination of feature engineering and deep learning techniques. This paper examines the amenability of the dual of a group's groupoid C*-crossed product associated with a Fell bundle, specifically within the framework of an action by a discrete group. We establish that the group must be amenable if and only if a specific cross-product C*-algebra admits a bounded approximate identity. Furthermore, we derive a characterization of amenable groups based on the nuclearity of crossed products formed by Fell bundles and discrete group actions. Finally, we explore the group's property of exactness in relation to the operator algebraic attributes of the resulting crossed products.

Prolate spheroidal wave functions are a well-established benchmark for testing numerical algorithms, finding utility across diverse fields such as optics, geophysics, and signal processing. This paper introduces a novel numerical technique for computing these functions, which leverages a recently developed algorithm to address a related boundary value problem. We demonstrate that the proposed approach yields highly accurate results and exhibits superior computational efficiency compared to existing methods.

We introduce a novel score-function-based denoising technique tailored for analyzing condensed matter crystals. This method employs a score function to identify and eliminate noise from experimental data, thereby reconstructing the underlying crystal lattice. By utilizing this score function as a drift coefficient within a stochastic differential equation, we develop a diffusion process that characterizes the distribution of atomic positions. The approach is further refined by incorporating a time-reversal mechanism to accelerate the denoising process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through simulations using synthetic data and show its successful application to real-world electron microscopy images of a two-dimensional material.

This paper introduces a Lagrangian method for deriving the ocean's kinetic energy budget, which is subsequently applied to an idealized, time-dependent, two-dimensional model. In this framework, the kinetic energy density is defined as the mean of the squared velocity, and its temporal evolution is governed by a Lagrangian partial differential equation. This equation accounts for changes in kinetic energy arising from advection, baroclinic and barotropic pressure work, and bottom friction. The study demonstrates that the proposed equation accurately reflects the time-varying kinetic energy distribution along Lagrangian trajectories.

We introduce a new thermodynamic scaling framework for glasses, grounded in the observation that the configurational entropy density, $\sigma$, follows a power-law relationship with the isochoric specific heat, $c_v$. This approach yields a universal scaling function for the glass transition temperature, $T_g$, as a function of composition, applicable across various systems. Furthermore, the scaling function incorporates a universal parameter, $\alpha$, which reflects the specific nature of the glass-forming liquid. We demonstrate that this parameter can be derived from the ratio of the isochoric specific heat to the isothermal compressibility, both evaluated at the glass transition temperature.

This semi-discrete version is derived from a Backlund transformation connecting the continuous mCH system to its discrete counterpart. The semi-discrete system is integrable, as demonstrated by the existence of the Lax pair. We demonstrate that spin-1 measurements are contextual, provided the system's quantum state is not restricted to a single wave function. This conclusion stems from a non-negative minimum variance (NMV) inequality, which holds validity for all contextual hidden variable models. The study establishes a direct correlation between the probability distribution of spin measurements and the system's wave function, showing that violations of the inequality occur specifically when the actual distribution diverges from the prediction made by the wave function. Consequently, the NMV inequality serves as a robust tool for identifying contextuality in spin-1 systems, even when the underlying quantum state is unknown.

Gravitational interactions significantly influence the spin dynamics of compact binaries, particularly when the system comprises a black hole and a neutron star. This study investigates the evolution of the neutron star's intrinsic spin by employing the first post-adiabatic approximation. We derive the associated energy and angular momentum fluxes and analyze how tidal effects influence the spin evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the component of the neutron star's spin orthogonal to the orbital plane undergoes secular changes, a phenomenon attributed to the non-coplanarity of the tidal potential and the neutron star's equatorial plane.

Object detection is a critical computer vision task, and YOLO has emerged as a leading one-stage approach by eliminating the need for traditional two-stage region proposal methods. This efficiency stems from YOLO's ability to directly predict bounding box coordinates and class probabilities for each image pixel. However, this method often struggles with accuracy, particularly when handling small objects. This paper introduces a novel one-stage detection strategy that integrates the YOLO framework with a super-resolution technique. By applying super-resolution to upsample low-resolution images before detection, the method enhances the accuracy of identifying small objects. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves superior performance compared to existing one-stage detectors.

Although quote collections are essential for research, they often suffer from errors regarding job titles and organizational affiliations. This paper introduces an approach to automatically identify and rectify these mistakes by leveraging social network data. We demonstrate that mapping authors to institutions via social networks significantly enhances the precision of existing quote database correction methods.

Decision trees and their ensembles are widely utilized in supervised machine learning due to their interpretability and efficiency. However, their performance is often constrained by the inability to capture complex, non-linear relationships within the data. This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance the predictive accuracy of decision tree ensembles by integrating them with a deep learning framework. The proposed method involves constructing multiple shallow decision trees, where the resulting leaf nodes are treated as input features for a deep neural network. This architecture enables the model to leverage both the inductive biases inherent to decision trees and those associated with deep networks. We evaluate this methodology on various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, demonstrating that the approach achieves superior performance compared to standard ensemble methods.

This study introduces a novel framework for assessing the suitability of machine learning models within an application ecosystem. We propose a method to quantify the alignment between a model's capabilities and its deployment environment, thereby enabling a more rigorous evaluation of model appropriateness. To achieve this, we define a set of criteria that characterize both the model and its surrounding ecosystem. We subsequently develop a metric to calculate the degree of fit between them. Our approach is validated through a case study involving a real-world application, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This study addresses the challenge of identifying and classifying emerging, infrequent data subclasses within continuous streams. We introduce a novel framework that integrates the strengths of both ensemble and instance-based methods. By utilizing the discriminative power of instance-based techniques alongside the adaptability of ensembles to handle concept drift, our approach effectively manages both rare and newly appearing subclasses. We evaluate the proposed method on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

Ptychography has become a vital tool for nanoscale imaging, particularly within the scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) domain, where it is essential for characterizing strongly scattering materials. This technique relies on acquiring a series of diffraction patterns from a sample via a focused probe, which is then scanned across the target. Although the probe's position is typically recorded during acquisition, the probe's precise shape is often unknown. This paper introduces a new method for reconstructing the probe's shape directly from a single ptychographic dataset. The approach utilizes a generalized probe model that incorporates both the probe's intensity profile and its phase. By employing a robust, iterative algorithm, the method simultaneously refines the probe's parameters and the sample's structure. The study demonstrates that this approach yields highly accurate reconstructions of the probe, even when the initial guess is poor. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is validated through its application to real experimental data.

In stochastic thermodynamics, the gauge invariance of the scaled cumulant-generating function (SCGF) is a fundamental principle. This work investigates the relationship between the SCGF's non-gauge-invariant components and the underlying stochastic dynamics. We demonstrate that the SCGF components, which correspond to the moments of time-integrated currents, are uniquely determined by the generator of the dynamics. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these SCGF components and the time evolution of the system's cumulants. These theoretical results are applied to analyze the SCGF components for both the standard Langevin equation and the fractional Langevin equation.

Reservoir computing, a neural network architecture, has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to process complex data streams efficiently. This study investigates the topological characteristics of reservoirs, specifically focusing on modularity and link density. Our findings indicate that a high modularity enhances reservoir performance, whereas link density exhibits a non-linear relationship with quality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this non-linear effect of link density can be mitigated by incorporating an appropriate amount of noise into the input signals.

We investigate the time evolution of a three-boson system featuring short-range interactions, confined in a three-dimensional harmonic trap, immediately following a sudden reduction in the trap's frequency. Our analysis reveals that the post-quench dynamics exhibit universal characteristics, which we examine across various initial interaction strengths. By utilizing both exact numerical methods and an effective two-body model, we identify a specific dynamical pattern in the three-body sector: oscillations in the three-body bound state energy, a phenomenon analogous to the well-established Efimov effect.

This article introduces a novel method for calculating Newtonian potentials, which is particularly effective for geometries exhibiting symmetry. The technique relies on Green's third identity, applied to a Laplace equation satisfied by the potential difference between itself and a spherically symmetric approximate potential. This approach yields expressions in terms of solid angles that are evaluated using a numerical quadrature scheme. The section on applications demonstrates the technique's utility in deriving potentials for geometries that are either symmetric or nearly so, such as ellipsoids, flattened spheroids, and toroids. Furthermore, the discussion extends to utilizing these results for determining self-intersections within multipole expansions.
